video.title: The Pros Grip Differently From You (with lesson examples)

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable drills such as hitting with only two fingers and progressive cues for grip tension and preparation.

problem.title_as_question: Why do players pivot the racket at the butt cap instead of the top of the hand, and how does proper grip innervation fix it?
problem.definition: Players often pivot the racket around the butt cap at the bottom of the hand rather than around the top V/palm, losing effortless lag, control, and hitting slot perception.
problem.target_player: Players struggling with forehand lag, pushing the ball, or lacking command over contact

quotes.text: One of the things I check for every player is whether their racket is pivoting here as they swing or whether it's pivoting at the butt cap here because so much of this lag elusive lag action
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And if you pivot the racket at the bottom of your hand, you will never uncover that effortless velocity control hitting slot feeling.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: But with the pivot at the top of the V, the V of your hand, the palm right here, now when I swing the tip of the racket back, the butt of the racket actually goes forward and out.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now a lot of the before footage you're watching here is mini tennis because the truth is you can tell just when a player's playing mini tennis whether they're pivoting the racket around the top of their hand
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: all of these players are going to go from this more kind of pushing style to a real hit with the racket head and they're going to develop velocity control and spin all at the same time.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now, our first and and most powerful tool for this is to take the bottom fingers off of the racket.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And players who pivot off the bottom a lot of times have these top references, these top haptic references disengage.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Maybe it's loose against the skin and it kind of wiggles and they fling the racket off of their bottom two fingers like this and they feel like they're getting velocity and spin
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, what we do is by forcing you to play with only two fingers, I am removing all of your haptic information down here and now I am forcing you to pivot here because you can't prevent it
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: So, this hitting axis right here, this back-to-front hitting axis pivoting at your palm, at the V of your hand perceiving that will fundamentally change your forehand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: isn't mapped onto the racket, then you'll never be able to organize this because you're basically playing blind. You're You're trying to create something, but you can't feel what you're creating when you do different things.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and then as we put our hand back on, as we kind of move off the two-swinger thing and put our hand back on, we're trying to innervate either the bottom of the palm here or the front two
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: when I use my bottom fingers, I can cheat the momentum of my racket head.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: if I have my bottom fingers around, I can cheat it and like wrist it up at the last second. Whereas with only two fingers, I can't cheat anymore.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: the wrist needs to be relaxed enough to bend backwards. Because if I have tension here, now I go here, and now the racket doesn't keep its momentum, and I swing forward, and I don't get anything.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: However, another great cue is just a feel for the same haptic signal that you got with the two finger.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: If I like squeeze these bottom two fingers to like keep pushing the racket forward, I can really mess up the swing... Now, I'm like actively hitting with slow twitch flexion of the wrist.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You're going to feel tension increase and your grip is actually going to be very firm at contact. But you you want to passively let that happen just with a desire not to drop the racket.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: I'm trying to use my fingers as sensory organs that let me use proximal mechanics to perceive the racket's momentum and then hit the ball with the racket's momentum.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: the first step to any forehand, first step of preparation, is not a unit turn, it is innervate the racket with the hand.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Sinner, Alcaraz, Federer often starting here and then wrapping their fingers around because the very first thing they're fishing for is that nestle the racket into the palm or nestle the racket into the V feeling.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Velocity is created proximally. Proximal meaning close to the spine. If you try to get velocity by by by hitting harder from here, that is going to break your signaling and it can even get you hurt.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: often your brain will move your reference down the handle for more leverage. So, if I'm swinging like this, but I have no great sense of my scap, my shoulder, my rotation, and I'm pushing the racket through like this.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: which means if we want more velocity, we don't go to leverage here to get more velocity. Instead, we go to proximal mechanics.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: We map the handle, we find a grip where he can actually perceive the hitting action, and that is the starting point for everything that we do on the stroke.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: when you're able to innervate your racket is practice makes you better, rather than the practice being kind of confusing, where the stroke feels the one way one day and then the different way the next day.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: Racket pivots around the butt cap at the bottom of the hand rather than around the top V/palm during the swing.
Stroke feels like a pushing action lacking effortless velocity, spin, and contact slot feeling.
Racket is flung erratically off the bottom fingers or ball dumps into the ground when artificial wrist manipulation is removed.

causes.statement: Top haptic references in the palm or V are disengaged or unmapped, leaving the player blind to top racket momentum.
Players use their bottom fingers to actively cheat and manipulate racket head momentum instead of letting proximal body mechanics guide it.
Wrist tension prevents the wrist from bending backwards freely in the backswing, halting racket momentum.
Prematurely squeezing the bottom two fingers produces active slow-twitch wrist flexion instead of passive elastic energy transfer.

angles.summary: When pivoting at the top V of the hand, swinging the tip of the racket back causes the butt to go forward and out, creating an equal and opposite racket flip.
Mini tennis footage exposes players pivoting off the bottom and pushing the ball versus hitting through the ball with the racket head.
Fingers should function as sensory organs that perceive racket momentum rather than as muscular tools trying to hit the ball.
Top pros like Sinner, Alcaraz, and Federer begin preparation by nestling the top haptic reference into the palm/V before wrapping their fingers around.
Velocity must be generated proximally from the spine and shoulder rather than shifting leverage down to the butt cap.

solutions.summary: Take the bottom fingers completely off the racket and swing hitting forehands with only two fingers to force the pivot to the top of the hand.
solutions.external_goal: Swing and hit balls cleanly without bottom finger leverage

solutions.summary: Transition from two fingers by putting the rest of the hand back on, innervating either the bottom palm or front fingers to feel the entire hand hitting.
Seek the exact same haptic feedback at the top of the hand that you experienced during the two-finger drill to cue wrist relaxation.
Stay relaxed early and allow grip tension to build passively toward contact solely from the desire not to drop the racket.
Start every forehand preparation by first nestling the racket into the top palm/V reference before wrapping the fingers around.
solutions.external_goal: Establish top handle contact before closing fingers around the grip
